newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm reform plans mauled by farm ministers.
newsitem.headline: EU farm reform plans mauled by farm ministers.

text.p: European Union farm ministers, fearful of angry farmers, on Tuesday fired a first salvo against the European Commission's plans to cut prices to prepare for enlargement eastwards.
During an informal dinner debate, nearly all ministers attacked the proposals which had earlier been presented by EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler.
"The mood was very negative. Only the British expressed any real support," said one farm minister.
But Fischler put on a brave face to the predictable reaction, saying the discussion had been constructive.
"Some misgivings and misunderstandings have been overcome," he told a news conference after the meeting.
Despite demands for higher compensation for income losses caused by the price cuts, the proposals had been accepted as a basis for discussion, he added.
"They came as a shock but I hope it will be a creative shock," said Luxembourg Farm Minister, Fernand Boden, whose country holds the EU Presidency.
Boden added that the proposals will be discussed in greater detail during a three-day informal meeting in Echternacht, Luxembourg, from September 7-9.
Published last week, the Agenda 2000 blueprint would cut dairy and cereal prices by 10 and 20 percent respectively but only partially compensate farmers for income losses.
German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert earlier told reporters that the proposals contained nothing positive for farmers.
Borchert has denounced the cuts as unnecessary and unacceptable, saying he will demand major changes.
French Farm Minister Louis le Pensec said the reforms would reduce farm production and incomes and criticised the Commission for failing to consult farmers.
Cutting support prices ahead of the next round of World Trade Organisation (WTO) negotiations would be a sign of weakness towards the United States, he told reporters.
But le Pensec supported the idea of fairer distribution of aid by limiting the amount any single farmer could receive.
Britain and Sweden were in a supportive minority.

British Farm Minister Jack Cunningham said the market oriented reforms moved in the right direction but needed to go much further in cutting subsidies so as to prevent an explosion in farm spending after EU enlargement.
"The Commission paper is a good start for discussion," Swedish Farm Minister Annika Ahnberg told Reuters.
Compensatory payments for cuts in support prices should only be for a limited period, cereals farmers should only be partly covered and milk quotas should be phased out, she added.
Irish Farm Minister Joe Walsh said Ireland accepted the need for changes but farmers must be adequately compensated for income losses. Price cut benefits must be passed to consumers.
